notes:
Slice "internet" (1994 to 2012, with the 2018-2019 retirement of P3P and DNT as the closing record). Scope: the HTTP cookie and its standards track (Netscape 1994, RFC 2109 in 1997, RFC 6265 in 2011); notice-and-consent law and policy in the US (FTC 1998 survey, HIPAA and COPPA, the FTC's 2010 and 2012 reports, the 2012 Consumer Privacy Bill of Rights) and the EU (Directive 95/46/EC, Safe Harbor, the ePrivacy Directive and its 2009 consent amendment, the 2012 GDPR proposal); privacy shocks (FT cookie exposé 1996, McNealy 1999, DoubleClick-Abacus 2000-01, PATRIOT Act, AOL 2006, Facebook Beacon 2007, Netflix Prize 2008); the first machine-readable privacy mechanisms (P3P full and compact policies, IE6 cookie filtering, the 2010 CMU 'Token Attempt' study, the 2012 Google/Facebook P3P bypass; Do Not Track from the 2009 prototype through Firefox 4, the W3C working group, IE10's default and the 2019 end); and the birth of VRM (Cluetrain 1999, Searls's 'Intention Economy' 2006, ProjectVRM 2006, the 2012 book). Extra array 'signals' describes P3P full policies, P3P compact policies and DNT: who speaks, what the signal says, its legal force and its fate. The key contrast for the IEEE 7012 story: in P3P the SITE states its policy and the person only sets preferences; in DNT the PERSON's browser speaks, but only one bit, with no legal force; neither lets the person proffer terms.

Method: sources found with web search; every quote was captured from the page text printed by tools/fetch-text.py and checked with --check. All quotes pass --check except three that the helper's paragraph extractor cannot see because the blog body is in div elements (Montulli's 2013 cookie post, used twice, and Soghoian's 2011 DNT history); those were verified against the full page text and are flagged in their notes. EUR-Lex returns an empty bot-challenge page to scripts, so EU texts were read from Internet Archive copies of the official EUR-Lex HTML, and the 2012 GDPR material from the European Commission Press corner's document API and a European Parliament copy of COM(2012) 11. The New York Times articles (2001 cookie history, 2006 AOL) were read via the Internet Archive. Apple's Safari 12.1 release notes were read from the JSON data file behind the script-rendered page. Several records were merged to stay near the 22-30 event target (RFC 6265 into RFC 2109; the In re DoubleClick ruling into the DoubleClick-Abacus event; HIPAA with COPPA; Firefox 4 with the W3C Tracking Protection Working Group; the White House blueprint with the FTC's March 2012 report).

Not verified or not read: the Financial Times original of 12 February 1996 (not online; a contemporaneous mailing-list repost of excerpts was used); Dean Hachamovitch's IEBlog post of 20 February 2012 (the MSDN original is not served to scripts and Internet Archive fetches kept failing with connection resets, so The Register's report quoting it is used); the FTC's 22 January 2001 DoubleClick closing letter is a scanned PDF with no text layer (read from the page image; its key sentence is also quoted in the In re DoubleClick opinion, which passes --check); the ACM WPES 2010 version of 'Token Attempt' (the CMU CyLab report copy hosted by the Future of Privacy Forum was used); the W3C APPEL preference-language draft (w3.org returned 403 late in the session); the exact date AOL posted its search file; the month the Cluetrain Manifesto went online; the publisher's own page for The Intention Economy (retail listings give 1 May 2012, not verified); whether Firefox 4 was the first browser to ship DNT (Internet Explorer 9 shipped DNT-related features in the same period; not verified, so no 'first' claim is made). The 'Microsoft revealed Facebook's P3P bypass' framing in the brief did not survive checking: Microsoft named Google; Facebook's header was publicised by Nik Cubrilovic (see myths). The optional Target pregnancy-prediction story (NYT Magazine, 16 February 2012) was not included.

Coordinates: laws at the legislature's seat or the stated place of signature ('Done at Luxembourg/Brussels/Strasbourg'); court decisions at the court; publications at the publisher or, where it matters, the place of writing (Searls at ETech, San Diego); online-only work at the author's institution; each has a locationNote, and most building-level coordinates are approximate.

events.title: Lou Montulli invents the web cookie at Netscape
events.place: Mosaic Communications Corporation (renamed Netscape Communications), Mountain View, California
events.summary: Around June or July 1994, Netscape engineer Lou Montulli, asked how a shopping server could remember a customer's cart, devised a way for a web server to hand the browser a small piece of state that the browser would send back only to that server. He later wrote that he had opposed the rival idea of a single unique identifier per browser because it could be used to track a user at every website. Netscape's preliminary 'Persistent Client State HTTP Cookies' specification described shopping carts, stored registration details and per-user preferences as the intended uses.
events.significance: The web's first memory mechanism was designed by the site for the site: the person's browser stored whatever the server chose to set, and the person said nothing.

sources.institution: Lou Montulli (personal blog, 'The irregular musings of Lou Montulli')
sources.title: The reasoning behind Web Cookies
sources.quote: The goal was to create a session identifier and general "memory" mechanism for websites that didn't allow for cross site tracking.
sources.note: Inventor's own retrospective account. The blog's post body sits in div elements that tools/fetch-text.py does not extract; the quote was verified against the full page text. Montulli also writes: 'I was very much against this concept because the unique identifier could be used to track a user at every website.' He dates the originating meeting to 'Sometime around July of 1994'; the New York Times (2001) says June 1994.

sources.institution: Netscape Communications Corporation (Internet Archive snapshot of home.netscape.com, 9 July 1997)
sources.title: Persistent Client State HTTP Cookies — Preliminary Specification
sources.quote: Shopping applications can now store information about the currently selected items, for fee services can send back registration information and free the client from retyping a user-id on next connection, sites can store per-user preferences on the client, and have the client supply those preferences every time that site is connected to.
sources.note: The specification itself is undated; the date given is that of the earliest archived copy used here, not of authorship (1994).

sources.quote: One day in June 1994, Lou Montulli sat down at his keyboard to fix one of the biggest problems facing the fledgling World Wide Web -- and, as so often happens in the world of technology, he created another one.
sources.note: Read via the Internet Archive; nytimes.com blocks scripted access.

events.title: The EU adopts the Data Protection Directive 95/46/EC
events.place: European Parliament and Council of the European Union, Luxembourg
events.summary: Directive 95/46/EC 'on the protection of individuals with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data' was signed at Luxembourg on 24 October 1995 and published in the Official Journal L 281 on 23 November 1995. Its Article 7 allowed processing only on listed grounds, the first being that the data subject 'has unambiguously given his consent', and Article 25 allowed transfers to third countries only where they ensured 'an adequate level of protection'. Member States had three years from adoption to transpose it.
events.significance: Made the individual's consent a legal ground for processing across Europe — the legal hook that later cookie banners, and eventually person-proffered terms, would hang on.

sources.title: Directive 95/46/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 24 October 1995

sources.note: EUR-Lex returns an empty bot-challenge page to scripts; text read from an Internet Archive copy (15 January 2025) of the official EUR-Lex HTML. The same text states 'Done at Luxembourg, 24 October 1995.' and, in Article 25(1), that transfers may take place only if 'the third country in question ensures an adequate level of protection.'

events.title: The Financial Times tells readers their browser is tracking them
events.place: Financial Times, Number One Southwark Bridge, London
events.summary: On 12 February 1996 the Financial Times published Tim Jackson's column 'This bug in your PC is a smart cookie', explaining that the leading web browser let companies track which pages an individual looked at, when, for how long and in what order. Jackson criticised Netscape for failing to tell users and noted that the only way to disable the feature was to edit or delete the cookie file by hand. Excerpts were reposted within days to the Cyber-Rights mailing list.
events.significance: The first mass-media warning that the web's memory had become an unseen surveillance channel, with no user-facing control.

sources.institution: Cyber-Rights mailing list archive (repost by John Whiting, 16 February 1996, of the Financial Times article)
sources.title: cr> 18Feb96 Tidbits — 'The way the cookie crumbles'
sources.quote: It allows companies to track which Web pages an individual looks at, when, for how long, and in what order.
sources.note: Contemporaneous excerpted repost headed 'Financial Times [London} February 12 1996 Tim Jackson: THIS BUG IN YOUR PC IS A SMART COOKIE'. The FT original (print, 12 February 1996) is not openly online and was not read; this repost is the earliest accessible text.

events.locationNote: The FT's London headquarters at the time (Number One Southwark Bridge).

events.title: RFC 2109 tells browsers to refuse third-party cookies by default
events.place: RFC Editor, USC Information Sciences Institute, Marina del Rey, California
events.summary: In February 1997 the IETF published RFC 2109, 'HTTP State Management Mechanism', by David Kristol of Bell Laboratories and Lou Montulli of Netscape, on the standards track. It defined 'unverifiable' transactions — requests, such as for embedded images, whose address the user had no chance to review — and said a browser must enable a cookie session in them only within the domain of the page the user chose, with any override defaulting to 'off'. The two dominant browsers did not adopt that default, and advertising networks built cross-site tracking on third-party cookies. When the IETF finally replaced the cookie standard in April 2011, RFC 6265 called third-party cookies 'particularly worrisome' but left browsers 'wide latitude to experiment' with their own policies.
events.significance: The first standards-body attempt to encode a privacy expectation into the protocol — and an early lesson that a privacy default nobody ships has no force; by 2011 the standard simply described the tracking regime.

sources.institution: RFC Editor / Internet Engineering Task Force
sources.title: RFC 2109: HTTP State Management Mechanism (D. Kristol, L. Montulli)
sources.quote: A transaction is unverifiable if the user does not have that option.
sources.note: Same section (4.3.5): 'User agents may offer configurable options that allow the user agent, or any autonomous programs that the user agent executes, to ignore the above rule, so long as these override options default to "off".'

sources.institution: The New York Times (Internet Archive snapshot)
sources.title: John Schwartz, 'Giving Web a Memory Cost Its Users Privacy'
sources.quote: The Internet Engineering Task Force was pursuing a different tack, however, recommending in 1997 that browsers be set to block any cookie that did not come directly from the site being visited.
sources.note: The same article reports that 'neither Netscape nor Microsoft took to heart the recommendation'.

sources.institution: RFC Editor / Internet Engineering Task Force
sources.title: RFC 6265: HTTP State Management Mechanism (A. Barth)
sources.quote: Particularly worrisome are so-called "third-party" cookies.
sources.note: Section 7.1 continues: 'These third-party servers can use cookies to track the user even if the user never visits the server directly.' and 'This document grants user agents wide latitude to experiment with third-party cookie policies'.

events.locationNote: Publisher's location (the RFC Editor was hosted at USC/ISI in 1997); lead author Kristol worked at Bell Laboratories, Murray Hill, New Jersey.

events.title: FTC survey: only 2% of data-collecting websites post a privacy policy
events.place: Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: In June 1998 the US Federal Trade Commission sent Congress 'Privacy Online: A Report to Congress', based on a March 1998 survey of over 1,400 websites. In its random Comprehensive Sample of 674 commercial sites, 92% collected personal information but only 14% posted any disclosure of their information practices, and only 2% of the sites that collected personal information had a comprehensive privacy policy notice. The Commission concluded that industry self-regulation had so far fallen short.
events.significance: The founding document of US 'notice and choice': the answer to surveillance became a policy the site writes and the person is expected to read.

events.title: Congress legislates privacy sector by sector: HIPAA and COPPA
events.place: United States Congress, Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: The Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (Public Law 104-191), enacted on 21 August 1996, required the Secretary of Health and Human Services to recommend standards for the privacy of individually identifiable health information within 12 months, and to issue regulations if Congress had not legislated within 36 months. The Children's Online Privacy Protection Act, enacted on 21 October 1998, required the FTC to make rules obliging operators of websites directed to children under 13, or knowingly collecting their data, to obtain verifiable parental consent before collecting, using or disclosing a child's personal information; the FTC's rule took effect on 21 April 2000.
events.significance: Instead of a general privacy law the US wrote sector-specific rules in which consent is a gate the data holder must pass — never terms the patient or family sets.

events.place: cluetrain.com (online); book edition from Perseus Books, Cambridge, Massachusetts

events.title: Sun's Scott McNealy: 'You have zero privacy anyway. Get over it.'
events.place: Sheraton Palace Hotel, San Francisco
events.summary: At Sun Microsystems' launch of its Jini networking technology on Monday 25 January 1999, chief executive Scott McNealy told reporters and analysts that consumer privacy issues were a 'red herring': 'You have zero privacy anyway. Get over it.' Wired News reported the remark the next day, with criticism from the FTC's consumer-protection director Jodie Bernstein and privacy advocates; the same day Intel had backed down over identification features in its Pentium III chip.
events.significance: The industry's fatalist position in one line — privacy as something already lost rather than something a person could assert.

events.title: DoubleClick backs off merging web-browsing profiles with names and addresses
events.place: DoubleClick Inc., New York City
events.summary: In June 1999 the ad network DoubleClick bought Abacus Direct, a direct-marketing firm holding names, addresses and purchasing histories on about 90% of American households, for more than one billion dollars, amid plans to link that offline data to its online browsing profiles. After a public outcry and an FTC investigation begun in February 2000, chief executive Kevin O'Connor said on 2 March 2000 that the plan had been a 'mistake' and that no merger of the databases would happen until government and industry agreed privacy standards. On 22 January 2001 FTC staff closed the inquiry, finding DoubleClick had not combined Abacus data with clickstream data. On 28 March 2001 a federal judge in New York dismissed a class action over DoubleClick's cookie tracking, holding that the DoubleClick-affiliated websites were parties to users' communications and had given DoubleClick sufficient consent to intercept them.
events.significance: The web's anonymous cookie profile and a person's real-world identity nearly fused; the backlash showed people cared, and the court showed whose consent counted — the website's, not the person's.

events.title: Brussels deems the US 'Safe Harbor' adequate
events.place: European Commission, Brussels
events.summary: On 26 July 2000 the European Commission decided, under Article 25(2) of Directive 95/46/EC, that the 'Safe Harbor Privacy Principles' and frequently asked questions issued by the US Department of Commerce on 21 July 2000 ensured an adequate level of protection for personal data sent to US organisations that signed up to them. Companies joined by self-certifying their adherence, with the Commerce Department keeping a public list.
events.significance: Europe's consent-based regime met America's notice-and-choice regime through corporate self-certification — a pact between institutions, not a term set by the individual.

events.title: Internet Explorer 6 starts blocking third-party cookies that lack a P3P compact policy
events.place: Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington
events.summary: On 21 March 2001 Microsoft announced that Internet Explorer 6, due later that year with Windows XP, would build privacy controls on the draft W3C Platform for Privacy Preferences. IE6 looked for a P3P 'compact policy' — a short string of tokens a site sends with its cookies — and, depending on it and the user's privacy slider, could deny, downgrade or accept a cookie. Its default 'Medium' setting restricted third-party cookies unless their compact policy marked them as fairly innocuous.
events.significance: The only mass deployment of P3P turned a site-authored policy into a gate key: sites learned they had only to send the right tokens, true or not, to get their cookies through.

sources.title: Microsoft to Deliver on Privacy Tools in Internet Explorer

sources.note: Same release: 'Depending on the situation, Internet Explorer might deny, downgrade or accept a cookie.'

sources.institution: Microsoft (IEInternals blog, archived on Microsoft Learn)
sources.title: Understanding Cookie Controls (IEInternals blog post signed '-Eric')
sources.quote: The default cookie setting is "Medium", a reasonable balance that allows first-party cookies (unless they're marked to be particularly impactful to your privacy) and restricts third-party cookies (unless they're marked to be fairly innocuous to your privacy).

events.title: The USA PATRIOT Act widens government access to records and internet metadata
events.place: United States Congress, Capitol, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: Enacted on 26 October 2001, six weeks after the September 11 attacks, the USA PATRIOT Act (Public Law 107-56) let the FBI seek court orders for 'any tangible things (including books, records, papers, documents, and other items)' in international-terrorism investigations (section 215), and extended pen-register and trap-and-trace orders to 'dialing, routing, addressing, or signaling information' of electronic communications (section 216).
events.significance: Showed that the data trails built for commerce were also available to the state — privacy terms set by companies could not bind government access.

events.title: The ePrivacy Directive: sites must inform users and offer a right to refuse cookies
events.place: European Parliament and Council of the European Union, Brussels
events.summary: Directive 2002/58/EC on privacy and electronic communications, signed at Brussels on 12 July 2002, included Article 5(3): storing information on, or accessing information stored in, a user's terminal equipment was allowed only if the user received clear and comprehensive information about the purposes and was 'offered the right to refuse such processing'. Strictly necessary storage for transmission or for a service the user explicitly requested was exempt.
events.significance: Europe's first cookie rule was an opt-out: the person could refuse, but only one site at a time and only on the site's terms.

events.title: W3C makes P3P a Recommendation: websites publish machine-readable privacy policies
events.place: World Wide Web Consortium (hosted at MIT Laboratory for Computer Science), Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: On 16 April 2002 the W3C issued the Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 as a Recommendation, edited by Massimo Marchiori with authors including Lorrie Cranor (AT&T). P3P let a website express its privacy practices in a standard XML vocabulary that user agents could fetch automatically and compare with preferences the user had set, so the user need not read every policy. The specification itself stated that it offered no technical way to make sure sites acted according to their policies.
events.significance: The closest ancestor of IEEE 7012 — but inverted: in P3P the site states the terms and the person's software only decides whether to accept them; the person never proffers terms of their own.

sources.title: The Platform for Privacy Preferences 1.0 (P3P1.0) Specification — W3C Recommendation 16 April 2002
sources.quote: The Platform for Privacy Preferences Project (P3P) enables Web sites to express their privacy practices in a standard format that can be retrieved automatically and interpreted easily by user agents.
sources.note: Section 1, Introduction, continues: 'Thus users need not read the privacy policies at every site they visit. Although P3P provides a technical mechanism for ensuring that users can be informed about privacy policies before they release personal information, it does not provide a technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies.'

events.locationNote: W3C's US host in 2002 was the MIT Laboratory for Computer Science; coordinates approximate (Technology Square, Cambridge).

events.title: AOL releases 20 million 'anonymous' searches; the New York Times finds user No. 4417749
events.place: The New York Times, 229 West 43rd Street, New York City
events.summary: AOL had posted about 20 million web search queries from some 658,000 users, each identified only by a number, hoping to help academic researchers; it then withdrew the file and apologised, calling the release unauthorised. On 9 August 2006 the New York Times reported that user No. 4417749, whose queries included 'landscapers in Lilburn, Ga' and people named Arnold, was Thelma Arnold, a 62-year-old widow in Lilburn, Georgia. 'My goodness, it's my whole personal life,' she said.
events.significance: Proof that a stream of intentions typed into a search box is itself identifying — 'anonymised' data held by the service offered the person no protection at all.

events.title: Doc Searls names 'The Intention Economy'
events.place: O'Reilly Emerging Technology Conference, Manchester Grand Hyatt, San Diego
events.summary: Writing from the audience at O'Reilly's ETech conference in San Diego, whose theme was 'The Attention Economy', Doc Searls published 'The Intention Economy' in Linux Journal on 8 March 2006. He argued that attention-based advertising was a seller-side idea and proposed instead an economy in which 'the buyer notifies the market of the intent to buy, and sellers compete for the buyer's purchase', illustrated by a skier broadcasting a car-rental request to the whole market.
events.significance: The first statement of the idea that the customer, not the advertiser, should originate the signal — the conceptual root of VRM and of IEEE 7012's person-side terms.

sources.title: Doc Searls, 'The Intention Economy'
sources.quote: The Intention Economy grows around buyers, not sellers. It leverages the simple fact that buyers are the first source of money, and that they come ready-made. You don't need advertising to make them.
sources.note: Post date 'on March 8, 2006' from the page's date field. Same article: 'In The Intention Economy, the buyer notifies the market of the intent to buy, and sellers compete for the buyer's purchase.'

sources.note: Establishes the venue from which Searls wrote ('this year's eTech conference, where I am sitting in an audience, writing this').

events.locationNote: Where the article was written (ETech 2006 venue); Linux Journal was an online/print magazine.

events.title: Facebook Beacon broadcasts off-site purchases — then retreats to opt-in
events.place: Facebook Social Advertising Event, New York City
events.summary: On 6 November 2007 Facebook announced that 44 websites, including Fandango and eBay, were using Beacon to send users' actions on their sites, such as purchases, to Facebook for display to friends. Beacon was initially opt-out: if a user forgot to decline, the action was shared. After weeks of protest Facebook switched it to opt-in, and on 5 December 2007 Mark Zuckerberg apologised — 'We simply did a bad job with this release, and I apologize for it' — and added a control to turn Beacon off completely.
events.significance: A default set by the platform, not the person, exposed purchases across sites — a vivid case of why the person needs a standing, portable term rather than a per-site opt-out.

sources.title: Leading Websites Offer Facebook Beacon for Social Distribution
sources.quote: Facebook announced today that 44 websites are using Facebook Beacon to allow users to share information from other websites for distribution to their friends on Facebook.
sources.note: Dateline: 'NEW YORK — Facebook Social Advertising Event, Nov. 6, 2007'.

sources.quote: The problem with our initial approach of making it an opt-out system instead of opt-in was that if someone forgot to decline to share something, Beacon still went ahead and shared it with their friends.
sources.note: Newsroom URL gives the month (2007/12); the day is from TechCrunch, 5 December 2007 ('in a blog post this morning'). Same post: 'We simply did a bad job with this release, and I apologize for it.' and 'Last week we changed Beacon to be an opt-in system, and today we’re releasing a privacy control to turn off Beacon completely.'

events.title: Narayanan and Shmatikov re-identify 'anonymous' Netflix Prize raters
events.place: IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy, Oakland, California
events.summary: Arvind Narayanan and Vitaly Shmatikov of the University of Texas at Austin showed that the Netflix Prize dataset of movie ratings by 500,000 subscribers, released with names removed, could be de-anonymised: with 8 ratings (two of which could be wrong) and dates within 14 days, 99% of records could be uniquely identified. Using public IMDb reviews as background knowledge they identified known users' records, revealing apparent political preferences. A preprint appeared on arXiv on 18 October 2006; the paper was presented at the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy in Oakland in May 2008.
events.significance: Showed that removing names does not make behavioural data anonymous — so protection has to attach to the person's terms of use, not to the data holder's promise of anonymisation.

sources.quote: With 8 movie ratings (of which 2 may be completely wrong) and dates that may have a 14-day error, 99% of records can be uniquely identiﬁed in the dataset.
sources.note: The 'ﬁ' ligature is as it appears in the PDF text layer. Abstract: 'We demonstrate that an adversary who knows only a little bit about an individual subscriber can easily identify this subscriber’s record in the dataset.'

events.title: Soghoian and Stamm prototype a 'Do Not Track' browser header
events.place: Indiana University, Bloomington, Indiana
events.summary: In July 2009 privacy researcher Christopher Soghoian, with his collaborator Sid Stamm, built a prototype Firefox add-on that added two headers to every outgoing web request, 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1' and 'X-Do-Not-Track: 1'. The idea replaced dozens of per-network opt-out cookies with one signal sent to every server, but it depended on advertisers choosing to honour it.
events.significance: The first person-side machine-readable privacy signal on the web: the browser speaks for the person, but only a one-bit request with no legal force.

sources.title: The History of the Do Not Track Header

sources.note: Inventor's own account. The post body is in div elements that tools/fetch-text.py does not extract (it returns only the quoted blocks, which include 'X-Behavioral-Ad-Opt-Out: 1 X-Do-Not-Track: 1'); the quote was verified against the full page text.

events.locationNote: Approximate: Soghoian was then a doctoral student at Indiana University Bloomington; the add-on was distributed online.

events.title: The EU 'cookie law': storing cookies now needs the user's consent
events.place: European Parliament, Strasbourg
events.summary: Directive 2009/136/EC, signed at Strasbourg on 25 November 2009, replaced Article 5(3) of the ePrivacy Directive: storing or accessing information on a user's device became lawful only if the user 'has given his or her consent', after clear and comprehensive information, except where strictly necessary. Recital 66 added that, where technically possible and effective, consent 'may be expressed by using the appropriate settings of a browser or other application'.
events.significance: Moved Europe from opt-out to opt-in and explicitly contemplated consent expressed by software on the person's side — the legal opening that browser signals, and later machine-readable personal terms, would try to use.

sources.institution: EUR-Lex, Publications Office of the European Union (Internet Archive snapshot)
sources.title: Directive 2009/136/EC of the European Parliament and of the Council of 25 November 2009
sources.quote: Member States shall ensure that the storing of information, or the gaining of access to information already stored, in the terminal equipment of a subscriber or user is only allowed on condition that the subscriber or user concerned has given his or her consent, having been provided with clear and comprehensive information, in accordance with Directive 95/46/EC, inter alia, about the purposes of the processing.
sources.note: Article 2(5), replacing Article 5(3) of Directive 2002/58/EC. Recital 66: 'the user’s consent to processing may be expressed by using the appropriate settings of a browser or other application.' Signed 'Done at Strasbourg, 25 November 2009.' EUR-Lex blocks scripts; read via the Internet Archive.

events.locationNote: 'Done at Strasbourg'; coordinates are the European Parliament's Louise Weiss building.

events.title: Carnegie Mellon finds a third of P3P compact policies are erroneous — many deliberately
events.place: CyLab, Carnegie Mellon University, Pittsburgh
events.summary: In a CyLab technical report dated 10 September 2010, Pedro Giovanni Leon, Lorrie Faith Cranor, Aleecia McDonald and Robert McGuire collected P3P compact policies from 33,139 websites and found errors in 11,176 of them, including 134 TRUSTe-certified sites and 21 of the 100 most-visited. Thousands of sites used identical invalid policies that had been circulated as workarounds for Internet Explorer's cookie blocking, and 98% of invalid policies left cookies unblocked under IE's default settings.
events.significance: Documented how a site-authored machine-readable policy fails when nothing enforces its truth: the site 'spoke', the browser believed it, and the person was misled.

sources.institution: Future of Privacy Forum (hosted copy of CMU CyLab Technical Report CMU-CyLab-10-014)
sources.title: Leon, Cranor, McDonald & McGuire, 'Token Attempt: The Misrepresentation of Website Privacy Policies through the Misuse of P3P Compact Policy Tokens'
sources.quote: We collected CPs from 33,139 websites and detected errors in 11,176 of them
sources.note: Abstract continues: 'including 134 TRUSTe-certiﬁed websites and 21 of the top 100 most-visited sites' and 'We found thousands of sites using identical invalid CPs that had been recommended as workarounds for IE cookie blocking.' and '98% of invalid CPs resulted in cookies remaining unblocked by IE under it’s default cookie settings.' The paper was also published at the ACM Workshop on Privacy in the Electronic Society (WPES) 2010 (DOI 10.1145/1866919.1866932; ACM page not read).

events.title: The FTC staff calls for a browser-based 'Do Not Track' mechanism
events.place: Federal Trade Commission, 600 Pennsylvania Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: On 1 December 2010 FTC staff issued the preliminary report 'Protecting Consumer Privacy in an Era of Rapid Change', which judged industry self-regulation 'too slow' and proposed a universal choice mechanism for online behavioural advertising — most practically 'a persistent setting, similar to a cookie, on the consumer's browser' — which staff said it supported under the name 'Do Not Track'.
events.significance: Put a regulator's weight behind a person-side signal — while leaving its meaning and enforcement to be worked out by industry.

sources.institution: Federal Trade Commission (Bureau of Consumer Protection)
sources.title: Protecting Consumer Privacy in an Era of Rapid Change: A Proposed Framework for Businesses and Policymakers — Preliminary FTC Staff Report
sources.quote: The most practical method of providing such universal choice would likely involve the placement of a persistent setting, similar to a cookie, on the consumer’s browser signaling the consumer’s choices about being tracked and receiving targeted ads.
sources.note: Executive summary, continuing: 'Commission staff supports this approach, sometimes referred to as “Do Not Track.”'

sources.title: FTC Staff Issues Privacy Report, Offers Framework for Consumers, Businesses, and Policymakers
sources.quote: The proposed report also suggests implementation of a “Do Not Track” mechanism – likely a persistent setting on consumers’ browsers – so consumers can choose whether to allow the collection of data regarding their online searching and browsing activities.
sources.note: Release date from the page's time element (December 1, 2010). Quotes the report: self-regulation efforts 'have been too slow, and up to now have failed to provide adequate and meaningful protection.'

events.title: Do Not Track ships in Firefox 4 and goes to the W3C for standardisation
events.place: World Wide Web Consortium, MIT (Stata Center), Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: Mozilla released Firefox 4 on 22 March 2011 with support for the Do Not Track ('DNT') header, a switch asking sites not to track the user for behavioural advertising. The W3C also chartered a Tracking Protection Working Group, co-chaired by Aleecia McDonald (Mozilla) and Matthias Schunter (IBM), to standardise 'a simple machine-readable preference expression mechanism ("Do Not Track")'; its first face-to-face meeting was held at MIT on 21–22 September 2011. The charter expressly excluded 'mechanisms for the expression of complex or general-purpose policy statements'.
events.significance: The person-side signal reached a mass-market browser and a standards body — but was standardised as a single preference bit, deliberately not a vocabulary of terms, the gap IEEE 7012 later set out to fill.

sources.institution: World Wide Web Consortium (Internet Archive snapshot)
sources.title: Tracking Protection Working Group Charter
sources.quote: The Working Group will produce Recommendation-track specifications for a simple machine-readable preference expression mechanism ("Do Not Track") and technologies for selectively allowing or blocking tracking elements.
sources.note: Snapshot of the charter as extended on 1 August 2012. Same page: 'The first face-to-face meeting will take place 21-22 September 2011 at MIT.' and 'The Working Group will not design mechanisms for the expression of complex or general-purpose policy statements.' Initial co-chairs: 'Aleecia M. McDonald, Mozilla Matthias Schunter, IBM'.

sources.quote: Support for the Do Not Track ("DNT") header that allows users to opt-out of behavioural advertising
sources.note: Same page: 'v.4.0, released March 22nd, 2011'. Whether Firefox was the first browser to ship DNT was not verified here, so no 'first browser' claim is made.

events.locationNote: W3C's MIT host site, where the working group first met; coordinates approximate. Mozilla was headquartered in Mountain View, California.

events.title: The Commission proposes the GDPR, with a 'right to be forgotten' and explicit consent
events.place: European Commission, Berlaymont, Brussels
events.summary: On 25 January 2012 the European Commission proposed a General Data Protection Regulation (COM(2012) 11) to replace the 1995 Directive. Its press release promised that consent would have to be given explicitly rather than assumed, a right to data portability, and a 'right to be forgotten' letting people delete data where there were no legitimate grounds to keep it. Three days earlier, in Munich, Justice Commissioner Viviane Reding had said the individual 'should be in the best position to protect the privacy of their data'.
events.significance: Europe's answer to the notice-and-choice era was stronger individual rights enforced by law — the regime into which person-proffered terms would later be offered.

sources.quote: A ‘right to be forgotten' will help people better manage data protection risks online: people will be able to delete their data if there are no legitimate grounds for retaining it.
sources.note: Read through the Press corner's document API (the human page https://ec.europa.eu/commission/presscorner/detail/en/IP_12_46 is script-rendered). Same release: 'Brussels, 25 January 2012 – The European Commission has today proposed a comprehensive reform of the EU's 1995 data protection rules' and 'Wherever consent is required for data to be processed, it is clarified that it has to be given explicitly, rather than assumed.'

events.title: Microsoft turns Do Not Track on by default in Internet Explorer 10
events.place: Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington
events.summary: On 31 May 2012 Microsoft announced that Internet Explorer 10 in Windows 8 would be the first browser to send the DNT signal by default. Some welcomed the move but others voiced concerns, and on 3 April 2015 Microsoft reversed course to follow the W3C draft's requirement that DNT express a user's own preference, saying that otherwise sites 'could argue that it doesn't reflect the users' preference, and therefore, choose not to honor it.'
events.significance: Exposed DNT's core weakness: a signal with no legal force is worth only what the recipient agrees it means — so the recipient got to decide.

sources.title: Brendon Lynch, 'Advancing Consumer Trust and Privacy: Internet Explorer in Windows 8'
sources.quote: Internet Explorer 10 on Windows 8 will be the first browser to have DNT on by default.
sources.note: Same post: 'Consumers can change this setting, but the default will be to send the DNT signal to websites that consumers visit.'

sources.title: An update on Microsoft's approach to Do Not Track
sources.quote: Without this change, websites that receive a DNT signal from the new browsers could argue that it doesn’t reflect the users’ preference, and therefore, choose not to honor it.

events.locationNote: Microsoft headquarters (Redmond); coordinates approximate.

events.title: Microsoft says Google's fake P3P policy bypasses IE privacy settings; Facebook does it too
events.place: Microsoft Corporation, Redmond, Washington
events.summary: On 20 February 2012 Dean Hachamovitch, Microsoft's vice-president for Internet Explorer, wrote that Google was circumventing IE's default privacy protection by sending a P3P compact policy reading 'This is not a P3P policy!', which IE treated as valid and so let Google's third-party cookies through. Google replied that complying with P3P was 'impractical'. The next day researcher Nik Cubrilovic showed that Facebook sent a similar non-policy ('Facebook does not have a P3P policy'), and Lorrie Cranor, a P3P author, later noted that no regulator had acted against any deceptive P3P policy.
events.significance: The end of P3P's credibility: when the site is the only party that speaks, and nobody enforces what it says, a machine-readable policy can be a machine-readable lie.

The article reproduces Google's header: 'P3P: CP="This is not a P3P policy! See http://www.google.com/support/accounts/bin/answer.py?hl=en&answer=151657 for more info."' and Google's statement that 'it is impractical to comply with Microsoft’s request while providing modern web functionality.'

events.title: Searls publishes The Intention Economy: customers who 'dictate their own terms of service'
events.place: Harvard Business Review Press, Boston, Massachusetts
events.summary: In 2012 Harvard Business Review Press published Doc Searls's book The Intention Economy: When Customers Take Charge, reporting on companies and projects fostered by ProjectVRM. Promoting it at a Berkman Center talk on 11 June 2012, Harvard described a near future in which individuals could control the flow and use of personal data and 'dictate their own terms of service'.
events.significance: Set out, six years after the idea's first statement, the programme that became machine-readable personal terms: the customer as first party, proffering terms that companies accept.

events.title: Washington backs consumer control: a Privacy Bill of Rights and an industry DNT pledge
events.place: The White House, Washington, D.C.
events.summary: On 23 February 2012 the Obama administration published 'Consumer Data Privacy in a Networked World', whose Consumer Privacy Bill of Rights began with Individual Control, and announced that advertising companies delivering nearly 90 percent of online behavioural ads, including Google, Yahoo!, Microsoft and AOL, had agreed to comply when consumers used Do Not Track. On 26 March 2012 the FTC's final privacy report endorsed Do Not Track and called on Congress to consider baseline privacy legislation; FTC chairman Jon Leibowitz predicted an effective Do Not Track option by the end of the year.
events.significance: The high-water mark of official faith in a voluntary person-side signal — no baseline law followed, and the promised DNT never became effective.

events.title: The W3C retires P3P and DNT; Safari drops the DNT switch
events.place: World Wide Web Consortium, MIT (Stata Center), Cambridge, Massachusetts
events.summary: On 30 August 2018 the W3C marked P3P 1.0 obsolete, noting that fewer than 6% of the 10,000 most-visited sites supported it and that no current browser acted on P3P policies. On 17 January 2019 the Tracking Protection Working Group closed, republishing its DNT specification as a Working Group Note because there had not been sufficient deployment or planned support. Apple's Safari 12.1, released on 25 March 2019, removed DNT support 'to prevent potential use as a fingerprinting variable'.
events.significance: Both machine-readable privacy mechanisms of the web's first era — the site's policy (P3P) and the person's one-bit request (DNT) — ended as failed voluntary standards, clearing the ground for a person-proffered, agreement-based design.

myths.claim: Cookies were invented to track people across the web.
myths.correction: Lou Montulli designed the cookie in 1994 as a per-site memory (shopping carts, logins, preferences) and says he rejected a single browser-wide identifier precisely because it would allow tracking at every website. Cross-site tracking through third-party cookies was an unintended consequence he later called 'the one gotcha' — though he also defended leaving third-party cookies enabled, on the ground that trackers would otherwise use less visible methods.

myths.claim: Do Not Track was a law: once your browser sent the signal, websites had to stop tracking you.
myths.correction: DNT was a voluntary HTTP header. The W3C never finished it as a standard — the working group closed in January 2019 for lack of deployment — and no law in the US required sites to honour it. Recipients decided what the signal meant: when Internet Explorer 10 sent it by default, Microsoft later conceded that sites could argue it did not reflect the user's preference 'and therefore, choose not to honor it'.

myths.claim: P3P let people set their own privacy terms for the websites they visited.
myths.correction: In P3P the website wrote the machine-readable policy; the person only configured preferences in their browser, which compared the site's policy with them and could warn or block cookies. The person could accept or refuse a site's stated practices but had no way to propose terms — the direction IEEE 7012 reverses.

myths.claim: The 2009 EU 'cookie law' requires websites to show cookie banners.
myths.correction: Directive 2009/136/EC requires the user's consent, after clear and comprehensive information, before non-essential storage or access on the user's device. It does not prescribe banners; its recital 66 says that, where technically possible and effective, consent may be expressed through the settings of a browser or other application. Banners were how sites chose to implement it.

signals.name: P3P 1.0 full policy (XML)
signals.body: World Wide Web Consortium (P3P Working Group)
signals.whatItSays: The website's own data practices — what it collects, for what purposes, for which recipients, how long it keeps data, whether people can access it and how disputes are resolved — in a fixed XML vocabulary published at a well-known location. The person's user agent fetches it and compares it with preferences the person has set; the person cannot send terms back.
signals.legalForce: None in itself. The specification offers 'no technical mechanism for making sure sites act according to their policies' and relies on laws and self-regulatory programmes for enforcement; no regulator is known to have acted against a deceptive P3P policy (Cranor, 2012).
signals.fate: Little deployment beyond Internet Explorer's cookie filter; fewer than 6% of the top 10,000 sites supported it in 2018, when the W3C declared it obsolete.

signals.name: P3P compact policy (HTTP 'P3P: CP=' header)
signals.years: 2001–c. 2018 (used by Internet Explorer 6 onward; defined in P3P 1.0)
signals.body: World Wide Web Consortium (part of P3P 1.0); implemented by Microsoft in Internet Explorer
signals.whatItSays: A string of three- and four-letter tokens summarising the site's cookie-related practices (purpose, recipients, retention, data categories), sent with the cookie. Internet Explorer's default 'Medium' setting used it to decide whether to accept, downgrade or block third-party cookies.
signals.legalForce: None. The browser had 'no technical means' to verify the claims; sites discovered that an invalid or even self-declared non-policy ('This is not a P3P policy!') got their cookies accepted.
signals.fate: Widely gamed: 11,176 of 33,139 sites had erroneous compact policies in 2010 and 98% of invalid ones left cookies unblocked; Google's and Facebook's non-policies were exposed in February 2012; retired with P3P in 2018, when no current browser acted on P3P.

signals.name: Do Not Track (HTTP 'DNT' request header)
signals.years: 2009–2019 (prototype July 2009; Firefox 4, March 2011; W3C Note January 2019; removed from Safari March 2019)
signals.body: Proposed by Christopher Soghoian and Sid Stamm; shipped by Mozilla and other browser makers; W3C Tracking Protection Working Group (Tracking Preference Expression)
signals.whatItSays: One bit, sent with every request: 'DNT: 1' — 'This user prefers not to be tracked on this request' — or 'DNT: 0' to allow tracking. The W3C draft added a 'Tk' response header for sites to say whether they complied, and an API for site-specific exceptions. It carries no purposes, conditions or terms.
signals.legalForce: None: honouring it was voluntary. Industry pledged in February 2012 to comply (with the White House saying the commitment would be subject to FTC enforcement), but the meaning of the signal — and whether a browser default counted — was left to the recipients.
signals.fate: Never became a W3C Recommendation; the working group closed in January 2019 citing insufficient deployment, Microsoft stopped enabling it by default in 2015, and Apple removed it from Safari 12.1 in March 2019 as a potential fingerprinting variable.
